math.title: Five brutal exam equations
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. Five different equations; do not reuse roots across letters.
statements: The system $\sqrt{2x+3}=y$, $y=x-1$, $y\ge 0$ has exactly two real solutions $(x,y)$.
After clearing denominators, $\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}+\dfrac{x-2}{x+1}=\dfrac{5}{2}$ has exactly two domain-legal real roots, both different from $\pm 1$ and $2$.
The equation $|x^{2}-5x+6|=x-2$ has a real solution strictly larger than $4$.
There exists a real parameter $k$ such that $x^{2}-2kx+(k^{2}-1)=0$ has a double root at $x=0$.
$\log_{3}(x-1)+\log_{3}(x+1)=\log_{3}(2x+1)$ forces $x=1$ as its only candidate, but $x=1$ is outside the log domain, so the equation has no real solution.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

From $y=x-1\ge 0$ and $\sqrt{2x+3}=x-1$, square to get $2x+3=(x-1)^{2}$, so $x^{2}-4x-2=0$, $x=2\pm\sqrt{6}$. Only $x=2+\sqrt{6}$ satisfies $x\ge 1$. Exactly one solution pair, not two.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Domain $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -1$. Set $u=x+1$, $v=x-2$ or clear directly:
$(x+1)^{2}+(x-2)^{2}=\tfrac52(x-2)(x+1)$.
$2x^{2}-2x+5=\tfrac52(x^{2}-x-2)$.
Multiply by 2: $4x^{2}-4x+10=5x^{2}-5x-10$, so $0=x^{2}-x-20=(x-5)(x+4)$.
Roots $x=5$ and $x=-4$, both in the domain and different from $\pm 1,2$. Exactly two legal roots.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Require $x\ge 2$. For $x>2$, $|(x-2)(x-3)|=x-2$ ⇒ $|x-3|=1$ ⇒ $x=4$ or $x=2$ (exclude $x=2$ from this branch). Also $x=2$ works separately. The only candidates are $2$ and $4$; none is strictly larger than $4$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Double root at $0$ needs $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=0$. Here $f(0)=k^{2}-1$ and $f'(x)=2x-2k$, so $f'(0)=-2k=0$ ⇒ $k=0$, then $f(0)=-1\neq 0$. Impossible.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Domain: $x>1$. Sum: $\log_{3}\big((x-1)(x+1)\big)=\log_{3}(2x+1)$, so $x^{2}-1=2x+1$, $x^{2}-2x-2=0$, $x=1\pm\sqrt{3}$. Only $x=1+\sqrt{3}>1$ is allowed. A real solution exists; the claim that there is none is false.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview: Hard radical/rational/absolute/parameter/log equations with domain traps and false uniqueness claims.

math.title: One brutal two-unknown setup — five counterfactual traps
math.context:
A workshop sells only type-$A$ kits and type-$B$ kits. In one week it sold a total of $100$ kits and booked revenue $€\,7100$. Type $A$ sells at $€\,50$ each and type $B$ at $€\,80$ each:
$$
a+b=100,\qquad 50a+80b=7100.
$$
The unique baseline solution is the factual starting point. Decide whether each counterfactual claim is true or false.
statements: The unique baseline solution is $(a,b)=(30,70)$.
If the type-$B$ price had been $€\,90$ instead of $€\,80$, with the same count $a+b=100$ and the same revenue $€\,7100$, then $b$ would have fallen below $60$.
If management had sold $10$ fewer type-$A$ kits and $10$ more type-$B$ kits than the baseline, revenue would have risen by exactly $€\,300$.
If total kits stayed $100$ but the revenue target rose to $€\,8200$ at the same prices, no nonnegative solution $(a,b)$ would exist, because an all-$B$ week only reaches $€\,8000$.
If prices stayed $€\,50$ and $€\,80$ but the shop sold the swapped mix $(70,30)$ instead of the baseline $(30,70)$, revenue would still be $€\,7100$ because only the kit labels changed.
math.solution_overview: Solve the baseline once: $(30,70)$. Each later claim changes one datum — a price, a quantity shift, an impossible revenue target, or a fake invariance under swapping the mix.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From $a=100-b$ into money: $50(100-b)+80b=7100$ gives $5000+30b=7100$, so $b=70$ and $a=30$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

New money equation $50a+90b=7100$ with $a+b=100$ yields $5000+40b=7100$, hence $b=52.5<60$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The shift is $(30,70)\to(20,80)$. Each replacement of an $A$ kit by a $B$ kit gains $€\,30$; ten replacements gain $€\,300$.

Check: $50\cdot 20+80\cdot 80=7400=7100+300$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

At these prices the maximum revenue with $100$ kits is $100\cdot 80=8000$. A target of $8200$ is unreachable for nonnegative $a,b$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At quantities $(70,30)$ the revenue is $50\cdot 70+80\cdot 30=5900\neq 7100$. Swapping the sales mix changes the money total; kit labels are irrelevant to the equation.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Mixed absolute, radical, rational, and quadratic equations
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. The five letters mix absolute-value, radical, rational, quadratic, and piecewise equations — different types on purpose.
statements: The equation $|x-1|+|x+2|=3$ holds for every $x$ in $[-2,1]$ and for no $x$ outside that interval.
The radical equation $\sqrt{x+3}+\sqrt{x}=3$ has unique real solution $x=0$.
The rational equation $\dfrac{1}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}=1$ has exactly one real root, namely $x=0$.
The quadratic inequality $x^{2}-5x+6\\ge 0$ holds precisely on $[2,3]$.
The mixed equation $|2x-1|=x^{2}-x-1$ has exactly two distinct real solutions.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $[-2,1]$ the left side equals the constant $3$. Outside, it is strictly larger than $3$. Solution set exactly $[-2,1]$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Domain $x\ge 0$. Isolating and squaring yields unique candidate $x=1$, which checks: $\sqrt{4}+1=3$. The value $x=0$ gives $\sqrt{3}+0\neq 3$. So the unique root is $1$, not $0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$\dfrac{2}{x^{2}-1}=1$ ⇒ $x^{2}-1=2$ ⇒ $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$, both legal. Two roots, not one at $0$. (At $x=0$: $-1-1=-2\neq 1$.)

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$x^{2}-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\ge 0$ on $(-\infty,2]\cup[3,\infty)$, not on $[2,3]$ (there the product is $\le 0$).

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Need $x^{2}-x-1\ge 0$, i.e. $x\le \phi_{-}$ or $x\ge \phi_{+}$ with $\phi_{\pm}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
Cases: $2x-1=x^{2}-x-1$ ⇒ $x^{2}-3x=0$ ⇒ $x=0,3$. Only $x=3$ is in the RHS-nonnegative set.
Or $2x-1=-(x^{2}-x-1)$ ⇒ $x^{2}+x=0$ ⇒ $x=0,-1$. Only $x=-1$ works in the region.
Exactly two solutions: $x=3$ and $x=-1$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview: Five different equation types: absolute sum, radical, rational, quadratic inequality, absolute-versus-quadratic.

math.title: Quadratic family with a parameter — critical cases
math.context:
For each real parameter $m$, define
$$
f_m(x)=x^{2}-2mx+(m^{2}-1).
$$
Decide whether each claim about this family is true or false.
statements: For every real $m$, the equation $f_m(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
The vertex $y$-coordinate of $y=f_m(x)$ equals $-1$ for every $m$.
If $m=2$, then the roots are $x=1$ and $x=3$.
There exists a real $m$ for which both roots are equal to $0$.
The axis of symmetry is $x=m$, so as $m$ increases the axis moves right, and at $m=0$ the axis is the $y$-axis.
math.solution_overview: Complete the square or read the discriminant in $m$. The roots are always $m\pm 1$; the vertex height is constantly $-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$\Delta=4m^{2}-4(m^{2}-1)=4>0$ for every real $m$. The roots are $m\pm 1$, always distinct.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis is $x=m$, and $f_m(m)=m^{2}-2m^{2}+m^{2}-1=-1$. The vertex height is constantly $-1$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$f_2(x)=x^{2}-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$. The roots are $1$ and $3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Both roots equal to $0$ would require $f_m(0)=0$ and a double root at $0$, hence also $f_m'(0)=0$. But $f_m(0)=m^{2}-1$ and $f_m'(x)=2x-2m$, so $f_m'(0)=-2m=0$ forces $m=0$, whence $f_0(0)=-1\neq 0$. Impossible.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Axis $x=\dfrac{2m}{2}=m$. It moves right as $m$ increases, and at $m=0$ it is $x=0$.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Twisted courier contract — one story, five what-ifs
math.context: A courier firm charges a base fee of $€\,12$ plus $€\,0.80$ per kilometre for daytime runs. Night runs use the same kilometre rate but add a flat night surcharge of $€\,5$ on top of the daytime formula. A client is comparing options for a single delivery of length $d$ kilometres ($d>0$). Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: A daytime run of $d$ km costs $C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d$ euros.
If the same distance were run at night, the night bill would be exactly $€\,5$ more than the daytime bill for every $d>0$.
There is a distance $d^{*}$ at which a daytime run and a night run would cost the same; solving $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ finds it.
If the firm waived the $€\,12$ base on daytime runs only (charging pure $0.8d$), then for a $20$ km daytime job the client would save exactly $€\,12$ compared with the original daytime tariff.
If distance doubled from $10$ km to $20$ km on a daytime run, the bill would also double, because both the base and the kilometre charge scale linearly with $d$.
math.solution_overview: One affine tariff story. The traps are a fake break-even equation that says $0=5$, and the false claim that an affine cost is homogeneous of degree one.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Base $12$ plus $0.8$ per kilometre is exactly $12+0.8d$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Night cost is $12+0.8d+5$. Day cost is $12+0.8d$. The difference is $5$ for every $d>0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The displayed equation is $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$, which simplifies to $0=5$. It has no solution. Day and night never meet under this tariff; the algebra shown does not find a break-even distance.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Original daytime at $20$ km: $12+16=28$. Pure kilometre charge: $16$. The saving is exactly the waived base $€\,12$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $10$ km the bill is $20$; at $20$ km it is $28$. Doubling distance does not double the bill, because the base fee is fixed.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Letter-heavy polynomial limits and end behaviour
math.context:
Let
$$
p(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0,
$$
be a real cubic, and define
$$
q(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{x^{2}+1}.
$$
Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}q(x)=+\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
If $p(1)=0$ and $p'(1)=0$, then $(x-1)^{2}$ divides $p(x)$, so $x=1$ is at least a double root.
For every choice of $a,b,c,d$ with $a\neq 0$, the horizontal line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $q$.
If $a=2$, $b=-3$, $c=0$, $d=0$, then $p(x)=x^{2}(2x-3)$, so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=\tfrac32$ is a simple root.
math.solution_overview: End behaviour of letter-coefficient cubics and of a cubic-over-quadratic. A common root of $p$ and $p'$ is a multiple root.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$q(x)\sim ax$ as $x\to+\infty$. If $a>0$, then $ax\to+\infty$, so $q(x)\to+\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The leading term $ax^{3}$ with $a>0$ tends to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, so $p(x)\to-\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A common root of a polynomial and its derivative is a multiple root. From $p(1)=p'(1)=0$ it follows that $(x-1)^{2}$ divides $p$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Since $q(x)\sim ax$, the values fly to $\pm\infty$ rather than to $0$. There is no horizontal asymptote $y=0$ when $a\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$p(x)=2x^{3}-3x^{2}=x^{2}(2x-3)$. The root $0$ has multiplicity $2$ and $\tfrac32$ has multiplicity $1$.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Two tangled exponential–log functions
math.context:
Define
$$
f(t)=2e^{0.1t},\qquad g(t)=8e^{-0.2t}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}).
$$
Also write $h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $f(t)=g(t)$ has the unique real solution $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.3}$.
$h(t)=\ln 4+0.3t$ for every real $t$, so $h$ is an affine function with positive slope.
If $t$ increases by $10$, then $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.
The product $f(t)g(t)$ is constant in $t$.
Because $f(0)=2<8=g(0)$ and $f$ grows while $g$ decays, one has $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.
math.solution_overview: Compare the two exponentials by taking logs. The intercept of $h$ is $\ln(1/4)$, not $\ln 4$; after the crossing point $f$ overtakes $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$2e^{0.1t}=8e^{-0.2t}$ becomes $e^{0.3t}=4$, so $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.3}$. The exponential is one-to-one, so the root is unique.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$h(t)=\ln 2+0.1t-\ln 8+0.2t=\ln(\tfrac14)+0.3t$. The slope $0.3$ is right, but the constant is $\ln(\tfrac14)$, not $\ln 4$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$f(t+10)=2e^{0.1t+1}=e\,f(t)$ and $g(t+10)=8e^{-0.2t-2}=e^{-2}g(t)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$f(t)g(t)=16e^{-0.1t}$, which still depends on $t$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

They meet at the positive time $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.3}$. For larger $t$, $f>g$. The claim that $f$ stays below $g$ for every positive $t$ is false.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Economic derivative of a tangled revenue path
math.context: A firm faces inverse demand $P(q)=120-4q$ for $0\le q\le 30$ (price in euros, quantity in thousands of units). Revenue is $R(q)=q\cdot P(q)$. Marginal revenue means $R'(q)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $R'(q)=120-8q$, so in particular $R'(5)=80$.
Revenue is maximised at the same quantity where $P(q)=0$, i.e. at the choke quantity $q=30$.
If output rises from $q=5$ to $q=6$, the linear approximation using $R'(5)$ overestimates the true revenue increase $R(6)-R(5)$, because $R$ is a concave quadratic.
At the quantity that maximises $R$, price equals marginal revenue.
Cutting price enough to raise quantity from $q=20$ to $q=21$ must raise revenue, because more units are sold.
math.solution_overview: Only the first claim is a direct derivative evaluation. The rest are economic traps: choke quantity versus revenue peak, concavity of $R$, MR versus price, and "more units always mean more revenue".
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$R(q)=120q-4q^{2}$, so $R'(q)=120-8q$ and $R'(5)=80$. This is the one straightforward derivative check.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$R'(q)=0$ at $q=15$. At the choke $q=30$, price and revenue are both zero — that is not the revenue maximum.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$R''=-8<0$, so $R$ is concave and the tangent overestimates increments. Explicitly $R(5)=500$, $R(6)=576$, so the true increase is $76<80=R'(5)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At $q=15$, marginal revenue is $0$ while price is $P(15)=60$. Price does not equal marginal revenue at the revenue peak.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$R(20)=800$ and $R(21)=756$. Quantity rises while revenue falls: past the peak, the price cut destroys more revenue on infra-marginal units than it gains on the extra unit.

So the statement is False.

math.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
math.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result is greater than 7%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result is greater than 3.4%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result is greater than 45%.
The probability that a tested deer receives a negative result equals 1 minus the probability that a tested deer receives a positive result.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result is greater than the probability that the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result, $P(T^+)$, was calculated in the overview using the Law of Total Probability, considering the prevalence of each subspecies and their respective probabilities of a positive test:

$$
P(T^+) = 0.08257
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $7\% = 0.07$. We have:

$$
0.08257 > 0.07
$$

.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

This claim asks for the joint probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result, $P(S_A \cap T^+)$. This can be found using the conditional probability $P(T^+ \mid S_A)$ and the prior probability $P(S_A)$:

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_A) P(S_A)
$$

From the overview, $P(T^+ \mid S_A) = 0.0572$ and $P(S_A) = 0.60$. Substituting these values:

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = (0.0572)(0.60)
$$

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = 0.03432
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $3.4\% = 0.034$. We have:

$$
0.03432 > 0.034
$$

.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

This claim asks for the posterior probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive test result, $P(S_A \mid T^+)$. This requires Bayes' Theorem:

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_A \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

From the calculations above, $P(S_A \cap T^+) = 0.03432$ and $P(T^+) = 0.08257$. Substituting these values:

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) = \frac{0.03432}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) \approx 0.415647
$$

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) \approx 41.56\%
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $45\% = 0.45$. We have:

$$
0.415647 \not> 0.45
$$

.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

The events of a tested deer receiving a positive result ($T^+$) and a negative result ($T^-$) are complementary events. This means that if a test is not positive, it must be negative, and vice-versa. For any two complementary events, their probabilities sum to 1:

$$
P(T^-) = 1 - P(T^+)
$$

This is a fundamental property of probability for complementary events.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

This claim compares the posterior probabilities of Subspecies C and Subspecies B, given a positive test result: $P(S_C \mid T^+)$ versus $P(S_B \mid T^+)$. We calculate each using Bayes' Theorem.

For Subspecies C, given a positive test result:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_C \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

We need $P(S_C \cap T^+)$. From the overview:

$$
P(S_C \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_C)P(S_C) = (0.169)(0.15) = 0.02535
$$

Using $P(T^+) = 0.08257$:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) = \frac{0.02535}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) \approx 0.3069
$$

For Subspecies B, given a positive test result:

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_B \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

We need $P(S_B \cap T^+)$. From the overview:

$$
P(S_B \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_B)P(S_B) = (0.0916)(0.25) = 0.0229
$$

Using $P(T^+) = 0.08257$:

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) = \frac{0.0229}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) \approx 0.2773
$$

Comparing the two probabilities:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) \approx 0.3069 \quad \text{and} \quad P(S_B \mid T^+) \approx 0.2773
$$

.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
This problem describes a population of deer composed of three subspecies, each with a different prevalence of a certain prion disease. A field test for the disease has a known sensitivity and false-positive rate. We are testing a randomly selected deer and observing a positive result.

Let $S_A$, $S_B$, and $S_C$ be the events that a randomly selected deer belongs to Subspecies A, B, or C, respectively. Their prior probabilities are:
$$P(S_A) = 0.60$$
$$P(S_B) = 0.25$$
$$P(S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $D$ be the event that a deer has the prion disease. The prevalence rates for each subspecies are:
$$P(D \mid S_A) = 0.02$$
$$P(D \mid S_B) = 0.06$$
$$P(D \mid S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $T^+$ be the event of a positive test result and $T^-$ be the event of a negative test result. The test characteristics are:
Sensitivity: $P(T^+ \mid D) = 0.90$
False-positive rate: $P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 0.04$

This means:
$P(T^- \mid D) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10$
$P(T^- \mid D^c) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 1 - 0.04 = 0.96$

To evaluate the probabilities involving test results, we first need to find the probability of a positive test result for a deer from each subspecies, considering its specific disease prevalence. This uses the Law of Total Probability for each subspecies:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) P(D^c \mid S_i)$$
Since the test characteristics are independent of subspecies, $P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D)$ and $P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D^c)$.
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c) (1 - P(D \mid S_i))$$

For Subspecies A:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(1 - 0.02)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(0.98)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_A) = 0.018 + 0.0392 = 0.0572
$$

For Subspecies B:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(1 - 0.06)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(0.94)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_B) = 0.054 + 0.0376 = 0.0916
$$

For Subspecies C:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(1 - 0.15)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(0.85)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_C) = 0.135 + 0.034 = 0.169
$$

Now, to find the overall probability that a randomly tested deer receives a positive result, we use the Law of Total Probability over the subspecies:
$$P(T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_A)P(S_A) + P(T^+ \mid S_B)P(S_B) + P(T^+ \mid S_C)P(S_C)$$
$$P(T^+) = (0.0572)(0.60) + (0.0916)(0.25) + (0.169)(0.15)$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.03432 + 0.0229 + 0.02535$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.08257$$
This is the base probability for many subsequent calculations.

math.title: Binomial courier audit — numbers only in the claims
math.context: A night courier logs 50 independent deliveries. Each delivery is on time with probability 0.8, independently of the others. Let X be the number of on-time deliveries among the 50. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The expected number of on-time deliveries is 40, and the variance of that count is 8.
The probability of exactly 40 on-time deliveries equals the binomial probability with n = 50, k = 40, success probability 0.8.
Because 40 is the mean, it must also be the single most probable value, strictly more likely than 39 and than 41.
If every delivery were certain to be on time, then the count would be 50 for sure and the variance would be 0.
After subtracting 40 and dividing by the square root of 8, the resulting number is exactly a draw from the standard normal distribution — not merely approximately.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expected value is 50 × 0.8 = 40. Variance is 50 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 8.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

That is exactly the binomial probability mass at 40 successes in 50 trials with success chance 0.8.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

For a binomial count the mode sits near (n+1)p = 40.8, so 40 and 41 can share the top probability. The mean need not be a unique mode.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

With success probability 1, every delivery is on time: the count is 50 almost surely and the variance is 0.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Centering and scaling gives mean 0 and variance 1, but the count is still a discrete binomial random variable. It is not exactly standard normal; normality is only a large-n approximation. That is the trap.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview: Binomial mean/variance/pmf in words and numbers; traps are unique-mode-from-mean and exact normality.
